title: An inexpensive, broadly transferable method to edit and regenerate plants

concept.text: The innovation would be a common, affordable method for making precise genetic changes in plants and recovering fertile individuals that transmit those changes to their offspring. It must connect three steps: choosing cells or tissues capable of producing a whole plant, delivering editing reagents into those cells, and regenerating successfully edited cells into fertile plants. Editing cells alone would not complete the capability.

The defining advance would be transferability across species and genotypes with little bespoke tissue-culture development. A method that substantially improves an already tractable laboratory variety would be useful, but the proposed breakthrough requires dependable recovery in a much broader range of plants, including difficult genotypes. Broad applicability and low laboratory burden are central parts of the concept, alongside precision and fertility.

significance.text: If achieved at the proposed breadth and cost, this capability would substantially expand access to causal plant genetics. Researchers could alter a gene and observe its effects in more of the plants they actually want to study, rather than relying primarily on amenable laboratory varieties. The December 2024 review documents technical and resource barriers that make this difficult, including specialized explants, demanding culture procedures, personnel requirements and controlled-growth facilities. Removing those barriers would also make established methods easier for smaller laboratories to adopt. This is a reasoned consequence of the proposed capability, not a demonstrated impact.

The revolutionary change would lie in turning a collection of species- and genotype-dependent procedures into a more widely usable experimental capability. It need not depend on inventing a new editing chemistry: better delivery and regeneration could make existing editing tools useful in many more biological settings. Its value would therefore extend beyond higher transformation efficiency in a single cultivar to a wider choice of experimental organisms and participating laboratories.

Conditional downstream possibilities include engineering crop traits, testing hypotheses in wild species and supporting conservation research. These are possibilities rather than automatic outcomes. Recovering a fertile edited plant does not establish that an edit improves agricultural performance or conservation prospects; each application would require additional biological understanding and development. Likewise, a broadly effective protocol would not imply that every plant can be edited or that the consequences of every edit are predictable.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a reliable connection between precise editing and whole-plant recovery across diverse genetic backgrounds. Delivery must reach cells that can regenerate, those cells must survive the procedure and form shoots and complete plants, and the resulting individuals must be fertile. Success at an intermediate stage, such as obtaining transformed callus, does not establish success at the later stages. The supplied review identifies failures of shoot formation despite transformed callus as a concrete example of this distinction.

The engineering barriers include genotype restrictions, the need to identify suitable explants, effective delivery into those explants, and complex tissue-culture workflows. Some approaches depend on immature embryos or embryogenic calli, creating demands for plant growth, material preparation, facilities and skilled personnel. A transferable method must reduce the amount of new culture development required for each plant while preserving dependable recovery of fertile edited individuals.

Morphogenic regulators and in-plant approaches provide routes toward overcoming these barriers, but extending regeneration in selected settings is only part of the goal. The unresolved integration challenge, as documented in the December 2024 account, is to combine broad applicability, heritable editing, reproducibility and simpler laboratory requirements in one practical method. The supplied evidence does not establish whether subsequent work has completed that integration.

current_state.text: Youngstrom, Wang and Lee’s review, “Unlocking regeneration potential: harnessing morphogenic regulators and small peptides for enhanced plant engineering,” was first published on 10 December 2024. It reports that morphogenic regulators and in-plant methods have expanded the range of transformable genotypes and improved transformation efficiency in various species. These are substantial advances toward broader access, but the review also describes persistent genotype dependence, complicated culture requirements and limitations in recovering heritable edits.

A specific limitation appears in the review’s discussion of AtPLT5: transformed calli in sweet pepper and Bok choy failed to produce shoots. This illustrates why successful transformation cannot be treated as equivalent to regenerating a fertile edited plant. The review’s conclusions also retain complex cereal culture and genotype dependence as challenges. These examples constrain the breadth demonstrated by the reported methods; they do not show that all morphogenic-regulator or in-plant approaches fail.

The supplied evidence assessment examined an identity-verified, untruncated alternative XML representation of the review’s full main text and references. Figure images, supplementary contents and the underlying primary studies were not independently inspected. The achievements and failures above should therefore be understood as findings reported by the review, rather than independently revalidated experimental results. No numerical efficiency, time or cost benchmarks are established by the supplied assessment.

The evidence supports a dated account of progress and remaining barriers in December 2024. Although the source artifact was retrieved on 11 November 2026, the supplied record contains no subsequent freshness-search evidence. It therefore cannot establish whether the proposed capability remained unachieved as of 1 November 2026 or at retrieval. This is a limitation on the temporal conclusion, not evidence that the review’s reported results are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent laboratories would apply one common protocol to a predeclared panel spanning cereals, dicots, woody plants and wild species, including genotypes known to be difficult. These are overlapping sampling categories rather than mutually exclusive lineages; panel design should make the actual taxonomic and genotype coverage explicit. Any permitted adjustments would be declared in advance so that extensive species-specific redevelopment could not be mistaken for transferability.
completion_criteria.label: Independent laboratories apply one common protocol across predeclared plant panel

completion_criteria.text: Proposed success criteria would include minimum recovery rates for fertile edited individuals, confirmed transmission of the intended edits to offspring, and minimum reproducibility across laboratories. Acceptable time and cost limits would also be specified before testing. The supplied record provides no numerical thresholds, and these criteria are an evaluation proposal rather than an established standard. Their purpose is to make reliability and affordability assessable instead of treating reporting alone as completion.
completion_criteria.label: Fertile heritable editing meets predeclared reliability and affordability criteria

completion_criteria.text: For every tested species and genotype, laboratories would report intended edits, fertility, inheritance, assessed unintended changes, failures, elapsed time and costs. Resource accounting should make the facilities, materials and labor needed to achieve the result visible. Reporting unsuccessful cases alongside successful ones would reveal where the method transfers and where it still requires further development.
completion_criteria.label: Report each species’ and genotype’s outcomes and full resource costs

completion_criteria.text: A convincing result would establish reproducible performance within the declared panel and operating conditions. Finite tests would demonstrate breadth, not literal universality. Claims of practical completion should retain the tested boundaries, including excluded plants, required starting tissues, allowable protocol adjustments and resource requirements. Agricultural or conservation effectiveness would remain separate application-level demonstrations.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible performance established within declared panel and operating boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BOT-03, whole-plant synthetic genome construction and rewriting, overlaps through the need to recover plants after genetic intervention. BOT-04 could make such experiments easier, but precise editing and regeneration do not establish the ability to construct or rewrite a whole plant genome. BOT-05, predictive plant biology from genome to whole-organism performance, could benefit from broader causal perturbation experiments; successful editing does not itself predict their organism-level consequences.

Roster-based synthesis: BOT-12, plant-wide communication and plasmodesmatal control; BOT-13, cell-wall growth and mechanical sensing; and BOT-17, cell-division planes and tissue patterning, overlap with the developmental biology relevant to regeneration. BOT-04 concerns recovering edited plants across diverse backgrounds. Each of those other concepts seeks an explanatory or predictive capability for a particular biological system, which regeneration alone would not supply.

Roster-based synthesis: BOT-01, nitrogen-fixing cereal partnerships; BOT-02, a carbon-concentrating photosynthetic system in rice; BOT-07, transferable desiccation tolerance; BOT-08, durable immunity; BOT-10, additional durable soil carbon; BOT-15, perennial grains; and BOT-16, control of plant–mycorrhizal nutrient exchange, are potential beneficiaries of more accessible plant engineering. BOT-04 would provide an experimental route for introducing and testing changes, while each retains its own biological and performance requirements.

Roster-based synthesis: BOT-06, reliable clonal seed reproduction, concerns a particular reproductive outcome, whereas BOT-04 requires fertility and inheritance without specifying clonal reproduction. BOT-14, programmable multigenerational epigenetic inheritance, concerns durable transmission of adaptive states; transmission of a DNA edit would not establish that capability. BOT-09, affordable preservation and recovery of exceptional plant diversity, shares an interest in recovering viable plants and reaching difficult species, but editing and regeneration are distinct from preserving diversity.

Roster-based synthesis: BOT-11, a testable causal explanation for the early radiation of flowering plants, has a more indirect connection. Broader access to genetic perturbation could support experiments relevant to evolutionary hypotheses, but a transferable editing method would not by itself explain a historical radiation. The concepts remain separate scientific objectives.

unresolved_issues: No supplied freshness-search record establishes whether later work completed the capability or materially changed the barriers after December 2024.
The evaluation panel, difficult-genotype selection, permissible protocol adjustments and numerical recovery and reproducibility thresholds remain unspecified.
Acceptable time and cost limits, and the laboratory resource assumptions underlying affordability, remain to be defined.
The scope and methods for assessing unintended changes remain unspecified.
The underlying primary studies, figure images and supplementary materials were not independently inspected in the supplied review; experimental details beyond that assessment remain unverified.

brief.title: Affordable gene editing across many kinds of plants
possible: Researchers could change a chosen gene in many more kinds of plants, grow fertile plants from the edited cells, and follow the change into their offspring. They could use a common, affordable method with little extra development for each species or variety.
why: Researchers could test what genes do in the plants they want to study. Smaller laboratories could take part with fewer demands for specialist staff, facilities and complex growing procedures.
This would widen the plants available for crop engineering, studies of wild species and conservation research.

sources.who: Christopher Youngstrom, Kan Wang and Keunsub Lee
sources.showed: Their review describes how genes that control plant development help edited cells grow into plants. It also covers methods that work directly on growing plants and reduce the need to grow cells in laboratory culture.
sources.quote: Optimizing  BBM / WUS2  expression cassettes has further enabled successful transformation and gene editing using seedling leaves as starting material.
sources.cited_for: The review explains progress toward editing more plant varieties and the remaining barriers to growing fertile plants.
sources.not_established: The reviewed methods do not establish a common, affordable route to inherited edits across a broad range of plants.

sources.who: Anshu Alok, Vidhyavathi Raman and colleagues
sources.showed: The team used genes that control development to grow new shoots directly on soybean plants. Their method reduced laboratory culture and produced inherited gene edits.
sources.cited_for: Soybean experiments connect simpler plant recovery with edits passed to offspring.
sources.not_established: Success in selected soybean varieties does not establish transfer across diverse species or affordability across laboratories.

sources.showed: A protein made by joining plant growth regulators improved recovery of whole plants in several cereals and citrus. The team also produced edited wheat plants.
sources.quote:
GRF4-GIF1
transgenic plants were fertile and without obvious developmental defects.
sources.cited_for: Growth regulators can help more plant varieties recover as whole plants after genetic modification.
sources.not_established: Improved plant recovery does not establish reliable inherited editing across the full range of plants sought.

sources.who: Michael F. Maher, Ryan A. Nasti and colleagues
sources.showed: The team induced new growth centres on plants, producing edited shoots that passed changes to offspring without conventional laboratory culture.
sources.quote: Meristems are induced that produce shoots with targeted DNA modifications, and gene edits are transmitted to the next generation.
sources.cited_for: Editing directly on growing plants can bypass conventional culture and produce inherited changes.
sources.not_established: Fertility failures and dependence on particular plants and gene combinations leave broad reliability unresolved.

shown: Alok and colleagues produced inherited soybean edits while reducing laboratory culture. Debernardi and colleagues improved whole-plant recovery across several crops. Maher and colleagues obtained inherited edits by inducing new growth directly on plants.
missing: A common method still needs to connect precise editing with fertile offspring across diverse species and difficult varieties.
Independent laboratories still need to demonstrate dependable results with little adjustment for each plant.
Broad success still needs to fit agreed limits on time, cost, facilities and skilled labour.

milestones.label: Independent laboratories use a common method across diverse plants
milestones.explanation: Independent laboratories would have to use a common method across a panel chosen in advance, covering cereals, broadleaf plants, woody plants and wild species, including difficult varieties. This would test transferability.

milestones.label: Inherited edits meet reliability and affordability targets
milestones.explanation: Fertile edited plants, inheritance and repeatability across laboratories would have to meet targets set before testing, within agreed time and cost limits. This would make dependable, affordable success measurable.

milestones.label: Every tested plant has complete outcome and cost reporting
milestones.explanation: Each species and variety would need reported edits, fertility, inheritance, assessed unintended changes, failures, time and full resource costs. This would reveal where the method works and what it requires.

milestones.label: Repeatable performance holds within clearly stated boundaries
milestones.explanation: Results would have to repeat within the declared plant panel and conditions, with exclusions, starting tissues, adjustments and resources stated. This would establish the method’s practical reach.

uncertain: Which plants and difficult varieties would provide a convincing test of breadth, and how much adjustment would still count as a common method?
What recovery rates, repeatability, time and resource costs would qualify as reliable and affordable?
Which unintended genetic changes should be assessed, and how?

page.title: Plant genome editing and regeneration across species
page.definition: A common protocol delivers editing reagents and regenerates whole plants from treated cells or tissues across species and varieties that resist existing transformation methods. The plants are fertile and transmit targeted DNA changes to offspring; recovery avoids sterile tissue culture and meets the stated bulk cost test.

goal.need: DOE's April 2024 report estimates that US laboratories transform 5,000–10,000 DNA constructs into crops annually, with about 200 constructs in bioenergy crops and 6–10 quality events needed per construct. Most plant genotypes resist transformation or regeneration, concentrating experiments in a few varieties. A transferable protocol would let gene-function experiments use a wider range of genetic backgrounds.

figures.caption: US crop transformation capacity reported in April 2024.
figures.note: A construct is a DNA design; the report identifies a need for 6–10 quality events per construct.

statements.body: US National Science Foundation and USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture
statements.quote: There is an urgent need for increased plant transformation capacity in the USA.
We need a method that is high-yielding, transferable between species and does not rely on tissue culture.

statements.body: DOE Joint Genome Institute Plant Transformation Workshop
statements.quote: Create methods that can be applied across multiple varieties within a species
statements.context: The passage states the workshop's genotype-independence research priority.

completion.title: One protocol produces inherited edits across plant species and meets PERSEPHONE's bulk cost target.
completion.criterion: One delivery-and-regeneration protocol, without sterile regeneration culture, produces fertile plants with sequence-confirmed targeted edits inherited by seed progeny in at least two species, including two previously recalcitrant varieties overall. An independent laboratory reproduces both species' results. Estimated cost meets PERSEPHONE's <US$200/event target at >1,000 events/year, including labor, reagents and capital amortization; its event denominator is an edited plantlet in soil. This joint cross-species test is an Atlas criterion.
completion.set_by: Atlas; an integration of ARIA's cross-species goal and ARPA-E PERSEPHONE benchmarks.
completion.basis: Searches of NSF PlantTransform, DOE BER and JGI reports, ARIA, PERSEPHONE, and plant-transformation standards, prizes and benchmarks found no joint completion test for cross-species heritable editing, independent reproduction and affordability. PERSEPHONE permits its metrics to be pursued separately. Their combination here is an Atlas test, not a field standard. Bulk event cost does not establish affordability for small laboratories, and two species do not establish universal applicability.

milestones.title: Edited plant tissues regenerate into fertile plants carrying sequence-confirmed targeted changes.
milestones.criterion: Regenerated whole plants carry sequence-confirmed target-site edits and produce seed. Monocots: Debernardi et al., published on 12 October 2020, recovered 30 wheat events from 32 infected calli; ten were sequence-checked, seven reached heading and were fertile, and three died. Eudicots: Alok et al., published in the issue dated 2 March 2026, recovered seed-producing soybean plants and genotyped nine parental plants.
milestones.set_by: Plant genome-engineering community convention: regeneration, target-site sequencing and fertility are experimental endpoints used by Debernardi et al. and Alok et al.
milestones.threshold_quote: GRF4-GIF1 transgenic plants were fertile and without obvious developmental defects.

milestones.title: Regenerated or directly edited plants transmit sequence-confirmed targeted changes to seed progeny.
milestones.criterion: Offspring sequencing confirms transmission of the parental target-site edit. Eudicots: Maher et al., first published on 16 December 2019, reported transmission in three independent soil-grown Nicotiana benthamiana cases without sterile culture. Monocots: Bhowmik et al., published on 12 May 2026, found inherited HvCMF7 edits in 24 of 30 barley offspring from two independent parents. The barley method used pre-existing Cas9 transgenic plants.
milestones.set_by: Plant genome-editing community convention: offspring genotyping establishes heritability, as applied by Maher et al. and Bhowmik et al.
milestones.threshold_quote: Meristems are induced that produce shoots with targeted DNA modifications, and gene edits are transmitted to the next generation.

milestones.title: A plant-engineering method yields five independent, sequence-confirmed heritable events.
milestones.criterion: The method produces five independent, sequence-confirmed heritable events. Relevant eudicot evidence includes Maher et al.'s three independent soil-grown cases. Alok et al. found edited soybean offspring in two of ten plants descended from one parent; sibling offspring do not establish independent parental events. The barley experiment described above tested offspring from two independent parents.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-E PERSEPHONE, DE-FOA-0003551, Category B, Table 4; the numerical threshold is tabulated. Model plants are permitted.

milestones.title: Two recalcitrant plant varieties are engineered at time and throughput comparable to an amenable crop.
milestones.criterion: Two recalcitrant varieties are engineered with iteration time and throughput comparable to an amenable crop. Monocots: GRF-GIF expanded the transformable wheat genotypes. Eudicots: a tomato study published on 4 June 2026 recovered SlDA1-edited shoots in M82 (4/41), Ailsa Craig (4/47) and Sweet 100 (2/24), with inherited edits. These studies do not provide the matched bioenergy-crop comparison required by this benchmark.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-E PERSEPHONE, DE-FOA-0003551, Category A, Table 3; the two-variety threshold is tabulated and was written for bioenergy crops.

milestones.title: Edited plantlets in soil cost less than US$200 per event under PERSEPHONE's bulk accounting.
milestones.criterion: A mature bioenergy-crop protocol has estimated event cost <US$200 at >1,000 events/year, including labor, reagents and amortized capital. Events are desired genomic changes realized in soil-grown plantlets. No qualifying cost result was located for either plant group.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-E PERSEPHONE, DE-FOA-0003551, Category A, Table 3; the cost threshold and accounting boundary are tabulated.

PERSEPHONE supplies no numerical equivalence margin for comparable iteration time and throughput.
